title: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
summary: How GitHub Actions turns a pull request into jobs and checks, how matrices and fail-fast schedule them, how to run exactly the right pytest subset locally, and why flaky tests break big suites and how to fix them.
outcomes: Explain what runs when you open a PR: events, workflows, jobs, steps, runners and required checks
Compute matrix job counts and predict the effect of needs, fail-fast and a missing pipefail
Select tests by node id, -k, -m and --lf, and read pytest exit codes
Compute how flake rate, suite size and reruns set the chance of a green run
Diagnose a flaky test as order, state or timing dependence and fix it with fixtures

lessons.title: What CI does when you open a pull request

blocks.md: You fixed a bug in a project you built from source in the previous course. You open a **pull request** (PR): a request to merge your branch into the project's main branch. Within seconds a row of checks appears under the PR, some yellow (running), then green or red. That machinery is **continuous integration** (CI): every proposed change is built and tested automatically, on clean machines, before anyone merges it.

Why not trust contributors to run the tests themselves? Because your laptop is one machine with one Python version, one operating system and whatever leftover files and packages you happen to have. A maintainer cannot see what you ran. CI gives everyone the same answer from a fresh environment, and it runs the configurations you do not have (Windows, macOS, older Python versions).

On GitHub, CI is usually **GitHub Actions**. Its vocabulary, from the official docs:

- **Workflow**: a YAML file in `.github/workflows/` that defines an automated process. A repo can have many.
- **Event**: an activity that triggers a workflow, such as a PR being opened or a push.
- **Job**: a set of steps that run on the same **runner** (a machine, by default a fresh virtual machine per job). Jobs have no dependencies and run in parallel unless you say otherwise.
- **Step**: either a shell command (`run:`) or a reusable **action** (`uses:`). Steps run in order and share the job's filesystem.

blocks.code:
name: tests
on:
  pull_request:          # opened, synchronize, reopened by default
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: python -m pip install -e ".[test]"
      - run: python -m pytest -q
blocks.caption: A minimal Python test workflow. Real projects add more jobs, but every workflow has this shape: when (on), where (runs-on), what (steps).

blocks.title: From a pull request to a merge button

nodes.label:
you push to
your PR branch

scenes.caption: Pushing a commit to a branch with an open PR fires a `pull_request` event (activity type `synchronize`; opening the PR is `opened`).
GitHub looks for workflow files whose `on:` section matches the event. Each match starts one workflow run.
The run's jobs start in parallel, each on its own fresh runner. Nothing from your laptop is there: each job checks out the code and installs dependencies from scratch.
Each job reports a status back to the PR. A step that exits with a non-zero code fails its job.
If the repo marks `test` as a required status check on a protected branch, the merge stays blocked until it passes.

blocks.md: Two details surprise new contributors. First, for `pull_request` events the code under test is not exactly your branch: GitHub checks out a **merge commit** of your branch into the current base branch (`refs/pull/N/merge`). If `main` moved since you branched, CI tests the combination. Second, a workflow is ordinary code from the repo, so the commands it runs are the best documentation of how the maintainers build and test the project.

A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

PRs from forks run with reduced trust. Per the GitHub docs, apart from `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets are not passed to runners for workflows triggered from a forked repository, and that token is read-only. Depending on repo settings, a maintainer may also need to click **Approve workflows to run** before CI starts on your PR. So a job that needs a secret (say, uploading to a cloud bucket) may be skipped or fail for you even though it works for maintainers.

blocks.title: One CI round trip, then a fix

scenes.caption: You push a commit. GitHub records a `pull_request` event and queues the matching jobs.
A runner picks up the job, checks out the merge commit, installs dependencies and runs the steps in order.
pytest exits with status 1 (some tests failed), so the step fails, the job fails, and the check turns red.
You read the log, reproduce the failing test locally (lesson 3), fix it and push again. A new run starts from a fresh VM.

blocks.md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

blocks.question: Your branch passes all tests locally. CI on your PR fails in a test file you never touched. Since you branched, `main` gained 20 commits. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: The CI runner is broken and you should ask a maintainer to rerun it
CI tests the merge of your branch into the current `main`, and your change interacts badly with something that landed since you branched
GitHub Actions only runs tests in files changed by the PR, so it must be a caching bug
Your local Python is newer, so CI should be ignored
blocks.explain: For `pull_request` events GitHub tests the merge commit `refs/pull/N/merge`. Rebase or merge the latest `main` locally and rerun the tests to reproduce. Blaming the runner first is how real failures get dismissed; and Actions runs whatever the workflow says, not only changed files.

blocks.question: A job in your fork PR fails at a step that uploads benchmark results using `secrets.BENCH_TOKEN`. The same job passes on the maintainers' pushes to `main`. Why?
options: Secrets other than `GITHUB_TOKEN` are not passed to runners for workflows triggered from forks
Fork PRs run on slower runners, so the upload times out
Secrets expire after each push
The workflow file in your fork is ignored
blocks.explain: The GitHub docs state that, with the exception of `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets are not passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository, and that token is read-only there. This protects the project from PRs that try to exfiltrate secrets.

lessons.title: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs

blocks.md: A real workflow has several jobs. Without extra keys they all start at once, each on its own runner. `needs:` adds an edge: a job with `needs: [lint, test]` waits until both finish successfully. If a needed job fails or is skipped, every job that needs it is skipped too, down the whole chain, unless it uses a condition such as `if: always()`.

A **matrix** turns one job definition into many. Each variable is a list, and GitHub creates one job per combination (the Cartesian product). Two OSes and three Node versions give $2 \times 3 = 6$ jobs, exactly the example in the GitHub docs. `exclude:` removes combinations, `include:` adds or extends them, and the docs cap a matrix at 256 jobs per workflow run.

blocks.code:
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [...]
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: true        # the default
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
        exclude:
          - os: macos-latest
            python: "3.10"
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps: [...]
  package:
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [...]
blocks.caption: A typical layout: lint and a test matrix in parallel, packaging only after both pass.

blocks.prompt: How many `test` jobs does this matrix create, and how many jobs in total does the workflow run when everything passes?
blocks.reveal: The product is $3 \times 3 = 9$ combinations; excluding macOS with Python 3.10 leaves **8 test jobs**. Add `lint` and `package` for **10 jobs** in the run. Each one gets its own fresh runner, which is why big matrices cost real CI minutes.

blocks.md: The timeline below uses a simplified model of one row of that matrix (one Python version on three OSes): lint takes 2 minutes, the test jobs take 6, 9 and 7 minutes, and packaging takes 1. Times are made up for illustration; real ones come from your project's run logs. Queueing delays for free runners are ignored.

blocks.title: Scheduling a run: parallel jobs, needs and fail-fast

scenes.caption: No `needs` between them: lint and all three test jobs start at minute 0 on separate runners.
`package` needs lint and test, so it starts when the slowest test job (windows, 9 min) ends. Wall clock is 10 minutes; runner time is 2+6+9+7+1 = 25 minutes.
Fail-fast (the default): windows fails at minute 4, so GitHub cancels the in-progress ubuntu and macos jobs. You learn about only one failure.
Because a needed job failed, `package` is skipped rather than run. With `fail-fast: false` the other OSes would finish, telling you whether the bug is Windows-only.
`max-parallel: 1` runs matrix jobs one at a time: 6+9+7 = 22 minutes of tests, package ends at 23. Same 25 runner minutes, more than twice the wall clock.

blocks.md: A red X on one matrix cell with grey cancelled cells next to it does not mean the other platforms passed. With fail-fast they never finished. Look at which job failed first; that is the one with the real log.

How does a step decide it failed? The runner looks at the exit code of the step's script. On Linux and macOS, a `run:` step with no `shell:` runs as `bash -e {0}`: stop at the first failing command. If you write `shell: bash` explicitly, it runs `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail {0}`, which also fails when any command in a pipeline fails. That difference matters for one common line.

blocks.prompt: A workflow step (no `shell:` key, Linux runner) is `run: python -m pytest | tee pytest.log`. Three tests fail. Is the step green or red?
blocks.reveal: **Green.** Without `pipefail`, a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command, and `tee` succeeded. pytest's status 1 is thrown away, so the job passes while tests fail. Fix it with `shell: bash` on the step (which adds `-o pipefail`) or drop the pipe and upload the log another way. The previous shell course covered pipefail; CI is where it bites.

blocks.md: Two more keys you will meet. `timeout-minutes` caps a job (default 360 minutes) so a hung test does not burn six hours. `concurrency:` with `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the older run in the same group when you push again, so only your newest commit is tested.

blocks.question: A matrix has `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]`, `python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]` and one `exclude` entry for `os: windows-latest, python: "3.10"`. How many jobs does the matrix create?
blocks.explain: Product $2 \times 4 = 8$, minus the one excluded combination gives 7. Each is a separate job on a separate runner.

blocks.question: Your PR shows `test (windows-latest)` failed and `test (ubuntu-latest)` and `test (macos-latest)` cancelled. What do you know about Linux and macOS?
options: They passed, because only Windows is marked as failed
They also failed, because cancelled means failed
Nothing yet: with the default fail-fast, GitHub cancelled them when Windows failed
They were skipped because they need the Windows job
blocks.explain: `strategy.fail-fast` defaults to true and cancels in-progress and queued matrix jobs when any one fails. Cancelled jobs did not finish, so they give no information. Fix the Windows failure or set `fail-fast: false` to see all results.

lessons.title: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest

blocks.md: CI is slow feedback: minutes per round trip, and every push re-runs everything. The fast loop is local: reproduce the failing test on your machine, fix it, and rerun only what you need. Large projects have tens of thousands of tests, so selecting the right subset is a core skill. This lesson uses **pytest**, the runner used by most Python and ML projects.

pytest first **collects** tests: it finds files named `test_*.py` (or `*_test.py`), and inside them functions starting with `test` and classes starting with `Test`. Each collected test gets a **node id**: the file path, then `::`, then class and function names, then parameters in square brackets for parametrized tests. `pytest --collect-only -q` lists them without running anything.

blocks.title: Selecting tests from a tiny project's 8 node ids

scenes.caption: `pytest --collect-only -q` prints every node id: 8 tests in two files. The three `test_scale` items come from one function parametrized with k = 1, 2, 3.
A full node id runs exactly one test. Quote it in the shell because of the square brackets.
`-k loss` matches names case-insensitively as substrings of the test, its class and its module, so everything in `test_loss.py` is selected.
`-k` takes a boolean expression. Adding `and not empty` drops one more test.
The full run: one real failure. pytest exits with status 1 and records the failing node id in `.pytest_cache/v/cache/lastfailed`.
`--lf` reruns only the last failures and skips files that had none. This is the edit, rerun loop while fixing.
scenes.output:
run-last-failure: rerun previous 1 failure (skipped 1 file)
1 failed

scenes.caption: Run a test alone and it can behave differently: `test_lookup` passed in the full run but fails by itself. Hold that thought for lesson 5.

blocks.md:
All outputs above are from a real run of pytest 9 on this toy project. The selection tools you will use most:

- `path` or `path::node`: by location, the fastest way to reproduce a CI failure (the CI log prints the node id).
- `-k EXPR`: by name substring with `and`, `or`, `not`.
- `-m EXPR`: by **marker**, a tag such as `@pytest.mark.slow`. Many projects define `slow` or `gpu` markers so you can run `-m 'not slow'`.
- `-x` stops at the first failure; `--maxfail=N` after N.
- `--lf` reruns only last failures; `--ff` runs them first, then the rest; `--sw` (stepwise) stops at a failure and resumes from it on the next invocation.

pytest's **exit code** is what CI reads. The docs define: 0 all collected tests passed, 1 some tests failed, 2 interrupted, 3 internal error, 4 command line usage error, 5 no tests collected, 6 maximum number of warnings exceeded (`--max-warnings`).

blocks.prompt: A CI step runs `pytest -k test_tokenizer_fast`, but someone renamed the test to `test_fast_tokenizer`. What happens to the step?
blocks.reveal: `-k` matches nothing, so pytest deselects everything and exits with **status 5** (no tests collected). That is non-zero, so the step fails. In our toy project, `pytest -k nosuchtest` printed `8 deselected` and exited 5. This is deliberate: silently running zero tests should not look like success.

blocks.md: Start from the CI log: copy the failing node id, run exactly that locally, then widen to the file, then to `-k` on the feature, then the full suite before pushing. For big suites, `pytest -n auto` from the pytest-xdist plugin spreads tests across one worker process per CPU.
Node ids, `-k`, `-m` and `--lf` turn a 20 minute suite into a 2 second loop. Use the narrow loop while fixing, then run the wider set CI will run before you push.

blocks.question: You are fixing one failing test among 4,000 and want each rerun to execute only the tests that failed last time. Which command?
options: `pytest --ff`
`pytest -x`
`pytest --lf`
`pytest -k failed`
blocks.explain: `--lf` (last failed) reruns only the recorded failures. `--ff` runs failures first but then the whole suite. `-x` still starts from the beginning and stops at the first failure. `-k failed` matches test names containing the word failed, which has nothing to do with results.

blocks.question: A parametrized test has node ids `test_pad[left]` and `test_pad[right]`. Only `right` fails in CI. Which command runs just that case?
options: `pytest tests/test_text.py::test_pad`
`pytest 'tests/test_text.py::test_pad[right]'`
`pytest -m right`
`pytest -k pad --lf`
blocks.explain: Parameters are part of the node id in square brackets; quote it so the shell does not treat the brackets as a glob. The bare function id runs both cases, `-m` selects by marker not parameter, and `--lf` depends on your local cache, which knows nothing about CI's failures.

lessons.title: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability

blocks.md: A **flaky test** sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code. Google's testing blog defines a flaky result as a test that exhibits both a passing and a failing result with the same code. The pytest docs explain why they are poisonous in CI: if a failure no longer reliably means the change broke something, developers stop trusting failures and start overlooking real ones.
Start small. One test flakes with probability $p = 0.001$ per run: it fails one run in a thousand for no reason. Harmless alone. Now put 1,000 such tests in a suite and require all of them to pass.

blocks.prompt: Assume each of 1,000 tests flakes independently with probability 0.1 percent per run, and the code has no bugs. Roughly what fraction of CI runs come back fully green?
blocks.reveal: Only about **37 percent**. The chance every test passes is $(1-0.001)^{1000} \approx 0.368$. On average one test flakes per run ($Np = 1$), so most runs are red even though nothing is wrong.

blocks.tex: P(\text{suite green}) = (1-p)^{N} \approx e^{-Np} \qquad\qquad P(\text{test reported failed with } r \text{ reruns}) = p^{\,r+1}
blocks.caption: Simplified model: each test flakes independently with the same probability p. Real flakiness clusters in a few tests and correlates (for example, a slow runner slows many tests at once).

blocks.title: Chance a bug-free suite comes back green

scenes.caption: At p = 0.1 percent, green probability decays exponentially with suite size: 0.905 at 100 tests, 0.819 at 200, 0.368 at 1,000 and 0.0067 at 5,000.

At Google's reported 1.5 percent flaky rate, 1,000 tests give an expected 15 flaky failures per run (the blog's own arithmetic) and essentially never a green run: $0.985^{1000} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-7}$.
One automatic rerun means a test is reported failed only if it fails twice: per-test rate $0.015^2 = 2.25 \times 10^{-4}$, and 1,000 tests are green 79.9 percent of the time.
Two reruns: per-test rate $3.4 \times 10^{-6}$ and the suite is green 99.7 percent of the time. Reruns are powerful against noise. The next scene shows their price.

blocks.md: Reruns hide noise, but they also hide real bugs that fail only sometimes, such as a race condition. Suppose your change introduces a race that makes a test fail with probability $q$ per run. With $r$ reruns it is reported only if every attempt fails, probability $q^{r+1}$.

blocks.title: Chance an intermittent real bug (q = 0.3) turns CI red

scenes.caption: Without reruns, a race that fails 30 percent of runs turns CI red 30 percent of the time.
Each rerun multiplies by 0.3: 0.09, then 0.027, then 0.0081. With 3 reruns the real bug gets through over 99 percent of the time.

blocks.md: Retrying until green is not fixing. The same math that removes noise also removes signal from real intermittent bugs, and concurrency bugs are exactly the ones that fail intermittently. Google's post makes a related point about its own fail three times in a row policy: it reduces false positives but encourages developers to ignore flakiness and delays finding real breakages.

The scale is real. Google reported (2016) that about 1.5 percent of all test runs gave a flaky result, that almost 16 percent of their tests had some level of flakiness, and that about 84 percent of observed pass to fail transitions in CI involved a flaky test. So when your PR goes red in a test you did not touch, flakiness is a serious hypothesis, but one you must check, not assume.

Small flake rates multiply across big suites: $P(\text{green}) = (1-p)^N$. Reruns buy back greens at the cost of hiding intermittent real failures. Fixing the flaky test is the only option without that cost.

blocks.question: A project has 400 tests, each flaking independently at 0.5 percent per run. About what fraction of bug-free CI runs are fully green?
options: About 13 percent
About 98 percent
About 50 percent
About 0.5 percent
blocks.explain: $(1-0.005)^{400} = 0.995^{400} \approx e^{-2} \approx 0.135$. The expected number of flaky failures per run is $400 \times 0.005 = 2$, so most runs have at least one.

blocks.question: A maintainer proposes `--reruns 3` globally to fix red CI. Which concern is most serious?
options: Reruns make pytest exit with code 5
A real race condition that fails 50 percent of runs would be reported only $0.5^4 = 6.25$ percent of the time
Reruns are not supported on GitHub Actions
Reruns change the order tests are collected in
blocks.explain: With 3 reruns a test is reported failed only if all 4 attempts fail. For a real intermittent bug with $q = 0.5$, that is $0.5^4 = 0.0625$, so about 94 percent of runs would be green despite the bug.

lessons.title: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing

blocks.md:
The pytest docs give the root cause in one sentence: a flaky test usually relies on some system state that is not being appropriately controlled. The common forms:

- **Order dependence**: a test relies on data left by another test, or another test fails to clean up. It appears when tests run in a different order or in parallel (pytest-xdist splits tests across processes).
- **Shared global state**: module-level dicts, environment variables, the current directory, files at fixed paths.
- **Overly strict assertions**: exact float comparisons or tight timing limits (`assert elapsed < 0.1`).
- **Threads and randomness**: background threads not joined at teardown; unseeded random numbers.

blocks.caption: The toy project from lesson 3. It passed in the default order and failed when `test_lookup` ran alone.

blocks.title: Same code, different order, different result

scenes.caption: Default order (file order): `test_register` runs first and leaves `relu` in the module-level dict.
`test_lookup` then finds `relu` and passes. The suite is green, but only by luck of ordering.
pytest-randomly with `--randomly-seed=2` shuffled the order in our real run: `test_lookup` ran first, found an empty dict and raised KeyError.
Across seeds 1 to 8 in our runs, seeds 2, 5 and 8 failed: the test is flaky under random order, and the seed reproduces it exactly.
After the fix (a fixture builds fresh state per test), both orders pass: no test reads state another test wrote.

blocks.md: **pytest-randomly** shuffles test order (by module, then class, then function), prints the seed it used (`Using --randomly-seed=...`), and resets Python's `random.seed()` before each test to a value derived from that seed. Pass `--randomly-seed=1234` to replay an exact order, or `-p no:randomly` to turn it off. **pytest-random-order** is a similar plugin. Running the suite in random order on purpose exposes order dependence before CI's parallel workers do.

blocks.caption: The fix: replace module-level state with a fixture. pytest builds a new `registry` for each test that asks for it. Built-in `tmp_path` and `monkeypatch` fixtures cover temp files and env vars.

blocks.title: Triage: is this CI failure real or flaky?

nodes.label:
run T's file and
CI's seed or order

scenes.caption: Start from the node id in the CI log and run exactly that test locally, on the merged code (lesson 1).

Fails every time: deterministic, most likely a real failure caused by your change. Fix it; do not rerun CI hoping for green. (A test that needs state from another test, like `test_lookup`, also fails alone, so confirm it passes on `main`.)
Passes alone but failed in CI: rerun with its neighbours, the seed CI printed, or `-n` workers like CI. Failing now points to order or leftover state.
Still passes: run it many times in a loop. Occasional failures point to timing, threads, unseeded randomness or the environment (CI machines are often slower than laptops).

blocks.md: Mitigations, roughly from best to worst: fix the test (fixtures, `pytest.approx` for floats, waiting on events instead of sleeping, joining threads at teardown); rewrite it at a lower level or delete it if other tests cover the behaviour, as the pytest docs suggest; and only as a stopgap, **rerun** (pytest-rerunfailures: `--reruns 3`, or `@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=3)` on one test) or **quarantine** with `@pytest.mark.xfail(strict=False)`, which the docs call rather dangerous to use permanently.

Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.
Flaky means uncontrolled state. Reproduce with the exact node id, order seed and loop count, find the state, and control it with a fixture. Reruns and quarantine are temporary and cost real signal.

blocks.question: A test passes alone, passes in file order, but fails about one run in five under `pytest -n 4` (pytest-xdist). Locally with `-p randomly` it also fails for some seeds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The test is too slow and xdist times it out
It depends on state another test sets up or leaves behind, so it breaks when the order or the worker process changes
xdist uses threads, which makes Python tests nondeterministic
Exit code 5 from xdist workers
blocks.explain: Failing under reordering and under parallel workers is the signature of order or state dependence. The pytest docs note that xdist spawns processes, not threads, and that tests relying on data from a previous test break when that test is on a different worker.

blocks.question: Your PR adds a feature, and an unrelated-looking test `test_download_retry` fails in CI once. Which response is best?
options: Add `@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=5)` to the test in your PR
Push an empty commit until CI goes green
Run the node id locally on the merged branch; if it passes, check whether it also fails on `main` or other PRs and mention that evidence in the PR
Set `fail-fast: false` in the workflow
blocks.explain: Gather evidence before labelling a failure flaky: reproduce on the merged code, then look for the same failure without your change. Silencing or repeatedly re-running a test you may have broken is exactly how real regressions get merged.
